newsitem.title: UK: Huge options position feeds FTSE index swings.
newsitem.headline: Huge options position feeds FTSE index swings.

text.p: As London' FTSE 100 share index climbs above 4,300 for the first time, dealers say a huge open position in the derivatives market is increasing nervousness and may be compounding cash market swings.
The 4,300 level on the blue-chip index is crucial for the position, taken in the largest single trade ever on the London International Financial Futures Exchange (LIFFE).
The position, which has an underlying value of 1.5 billion pounds ($2.4 billion), was taken by an unknown investor last November when the index stood at 3,935.

It was designed to protect the investor against any fall in the value of shares. But as the market has continued to climb, it has prompted rapid hedging adjustments which are helping to exaggerate the daily swings in the stock index.

"This huge position in the market is making it more volatile and could explain why the cash market is gyrating far more than is usual," said the head of derivative sales at one leading investment bank.
The trade was thought to be for a British life assurance company trying to lock in the value of its portfolio.
But as well as buying downside protection through derivatives, the investor chose to cut the cost of the deal via a "cylinder" trade. This involves trading both call and put options at the same time.

This meant the trade carried a risk of limiting profits if the FTSE rose above 4,300, a level which was then 400 points away, and the investor may now be looking to adjust this position to prevent losses running up.
"As we approached 4,300 the hedge on this position would be moving rapidly," said the head of derivative sales, who declined to be named.
Increased options activity can compound swings in the underlying index, causing investors to worry that nervousness at such high levels may signal the end of a rally.

A measure of how quickly the main FTSE 100 index of British shares is moving around over 10-day periods shows that volatility rose to 19 percent in mid-December before falling to seven percent and then doubling again to current levels of around 14 percent.

The huge position still open on LIFFE involved selling 35,000 June 4300 call option contracts and buying 35,000 June 3300 put options at the same time. The sale of the calls is used to offset the cost of the puts.

"Here is a strategy which gives you downside protection in case of emergencies, and it may cost you nothing," said one options trader. "It's attractive because fund managers like protection to be cheap or free, otherwise they will not have it at all."
A looming general election, signs of inflationary pressures in the economy and the growing unpredictability in the U.S. stock market are all seen as potential dangers for British equities.
"Fund managers are worried that if market sentiment suddenly turns around, all the profits from their shareholdings over the last 12 months may be wiped out," said one options trader.

Assuming the investor is holding a portfolio of stock, if the FTSE falls by over 20 percent in the next five months to the expiry date of the options, the losses from the portfolio can be offset to some extent by a rise in the value of the puts.
The investor would make 350,000 pounds from the puts for every point the FTSE falls below 3,300.

But in selling the calls to pay for this protection, the investor has sold his right to participate fully in a market rally above 4,300. Through the calls, the investor loses 350,000 pounds for every point the index rises above 4,300.

"One assumes that the investor has a basket of stocks which will perform if the market keeps on rising. But he must worry that if the market continues up he will be losing more than he makes," said one trader.

Since November, derivatives traders say they have seen a growing number of "cylinder" trades but the bulk of them are thought to have been executed in the relative secrecy and flexibility of the OTC (over-the-counter) market.

"The number of these types of trades we're seeing is making the market very jumpy," said one trader. "And they are continuing to be done through the OTC market, where there could be another 5-10 billion sterling invested in the same sort of way." --London Newsroom, +44 171 542 4027 ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
